{{Short description|Revelation of secrets to unauthorized parties}}
{{distinguish|whistleblowing}}
{{More citations needed|date=February 2013}}
'''Information leakage''' happens whenever a system that is designed to be closed to an [[eavesdropper]] reveals some information to unauthorized parties nonetheless. In other words, information leakage occurs when secret information correlates with, or can be correlated with, observable information. For example, when designing an encrypted [[instant messaging]] network, a [[computer network engineering|network engineer]] without the capacity to crack [[encryption]] codes could see when messages are transmitted, even if they could not read them.

== Risk vectors ==
A modern example of information leakage is the leakage of secret information via [[data compression]], by using variations in [[data compression ratio]] to reveal correlations between known (or deliberately injected) [[plaintext]] and secret data combined in a single compressed [[data stream|stream]].<ref>{{Cite book | last1 = Kelsey | first1 = J. | chapter = Compression and Information Leakage of Plaintext | doi = 10.1007/3-540-45661-9_21 | title = Fast Software Encryption | series = Lecture Notes in Computer Science | volume = 2365 | pages = 263–276 | year = 2002 | isbn = 978-3-540-44009-3 | url = https://www.iacr.org/cryptodb/data/paper.php?pubkey=3091}}</ref> Another example is the key leakage that can occur when using some [[public-key cryptography|public-key systems]] when [[cryptographic nonce]] values used in [[digital signature|signing operations]] are insufficiently random.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Rembovsky|first1=Anatoly |last2=Ashikhmin|first2=Alexander|last3=Kozmin|first3=Vladimir|last4=Smolskiy|first4=Sergey |date=2009 |chapter=Methods and Equipment for Protection Against Information Leakage Via CEE Channels |title=Radio Monitoring: Problems, Methods and Equipment |pages=471–496|location=Boston |publisher=Springer |doi=10.1007/978-0-387-98100-0_12|isbn=978-0-387-98099-7}}</ref> Bad randomness cannot protect proper functioning of a cryptographic system, even in a benign circumstance, it can easily produce crackable keys that cause key leakage.<ref>{{Cite web|last1=Schneier|first1=Bruce|last2=Fredrikson|first2=Matthew|last3=Kohno|first3=Tadayoshi|last4=Ristenpart|first4=Thomas|date=2015|title=Surreptitiously Weakening Cryptographic Systems|url=https://eprint.iacr.org/2015/097|url-status=live|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190414143224/https://eprint.iacr.org/2015/097|archive-date=April 14, 2019|website=Schneier on Security}} [https://www.schneier.com/blog/archives/2015/02/surreptitiously_1.html Alt URL]</ref>{{citation needed|date=September 2012}}

Information leakage can sometimes be deliberate: for example, an algorithmic converter may be shipped that intentionally leaks small amounts of information, in order to provide its creator with the ability to intercept the users' messages, while still allowing the user to maintain an illusion that the system is secure. This sort of deliberate leakage is sometimes known as a [[subliminal channel]].<ref>{{cite web|url=http://web.mit.edu/6.857/OldStuff/Fall02/handouts/L09-dss.pdf|title=6.857 Computer and Network Security Lecture Notes 9: DSA/DSS, RSA, chosen-ciphertext attack|author=Ron Rivest|date=October 3, 2002|publisher=MIT|access-date=2012-09-14}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal | doi=10.1155/2018/5823439 | doi-access=free | title=A Data Leakage Prevention Method Based on the Reduction of Confidential and Context Terms for Smart Mobile Devices | year=2018 | last1=Yu | first1=Xiang | last2=Tian | first2=Zhihong | last3=Qiu | first3=Jing | last4=Jiang | first4=Feng | journal=Wireless Communications and Mobile Computing | volume=2018 | pages=1–11 }}</ref>

Generally, only very advanced systems employ defences against information leakage.

Commonly implemented countermeasures included:

* Use [[steganography]] to hide the fact that a message is transmitted at all.
* Use [[chaffing]] to make it unclear to whom messages are transmitted (but this does not hide from others the fact that messages are transmitted).
* For busy re-transmitting [[proxy server|proxies]], such as a [[Mixmaster anonymous remailer|Mixmaster]] node: randomly delay and shuffle the order of outbound packets. This assists in disguising a given message's path, especially if there are multiple, popular forwarding nodes, such as are employed with Mixmaster mail forwarding.
* When a data value is no longer going to be used, erase it from the memory.
